title: Sendagaya Runs Three Different Schools — Which One Is for You?
summary: Three schools, nearly the same name, one group. They are not branches of each other — each runs a different track, and the wrong one costs you a year.
body_html:
Search for Sendagaya and you get three schools whose names differ by a word: Sendagaya Japanese School, Sendagaya Japanese Institute, Sendagaya Language School.

They are one group. They are not three locations of the same school, and the choice between them is not a matter of preference. Each runs a different track, with a different destination.

Sendagaya Japanese School: the university-preparation route

This one runs a preparatory education course, and the course is accredited by the Ministry of Education. [source:1] Intakes are April and October, with a stated capacity of 1,728. [source:1]

The accreditation is the whole point, and it solves a specific problem.

Japanese universities require 12 years of prior schooling. [source:1] If your home country's system runs 10 or 11 years, you do not meet that on paper — and completing an accredited preparatory course makes university entry in Japan possible for you. [source:1] The school states that only around 30 schools nationwide hold this accreditation. [source:1]

So this is the only one of the three that fixes an eligibility gap rather than a language gap. If you have 11 years of schooling behind you, the other two cannot help you get into a Japanese university no matter how good your Japanese becomes. [source:1]

Course length follows your intake: 2 years from April, 1 year 6 months from October. [source:1]

The teaching reflects the destination. Alongside Japanese, it covers EJU and JLPT preparation and the basic subjects those exams test in Japanese, plus the written statement of purpose and the interview. [source:1] Most universities and vocational schools require that statement of purpose at application. [source:1]

Sendagaya Japanese Institute: the graduate school route

Different destination, different course. This one is built for graduate school entry, with intakes in April, July, October and January, and a capacity of 900. [source:2]

Four intakes instead of two is the visible difference. The invisible one matters more.

The school states that entering this course requires a certain level of kanji ability, and directs applicants from non-kanji backgrounds to ask about the preparatory course instead. [source:2]

Read that as what it is: a filter, stated up front. If you are coming from a non-kanji-using country, this course is probably not your entry point, and the school is telling you so before you apply rather than after.

What it teaches is narrower and more advanced than general Japanese — writing logically for the entrance essay, for post-admission reports, and for a master's thesis, with repeated practice at writing to a set length under time pressure. [source:2]

Course length again follows the intake: 2 years from April, 1 year 9 months from July, 1 year 6 months from October, 1 year 3 months from January. [source:2]

Sendagaya Language School: the employment route

The third runs an employment-track course, with intakes in April, July and October and a capacity of 100. [source:3]

Note the size against the other two. A course for 100 students sits alongside one for 1,728 and one for 900. [source:3] [source:1] [source:2] Whatever else that implies, the employment track is the small, specialised one in this group — not the default.

If your plan is to work in Japan rather than to enrol somewhere, this is the one aimed at you, and the other two are aimed somewhere else.

The pattern hiding in the course lengths

Look at the lengths again across all three: 2 years from April, 1 year 9 months from July, 1 year 6 months from October, 1 year 3 months from January. [source:1] [source:2] [source:3]

Every one of them ends at the same point in the academic year. The intake you pick does not change when you finish — it changes how long you get.

That reframes the decision. A later intake is a shorter and therefore cheaper course, but you sit the same entrance exams with less preparation behind you. An April start buys you the most runway. January buys the least and costs the least. Neither is better; they are different trades, and the school is not making the choice for you.

How to choose between them

  • 10 or 11 years of schooling? [source:1] Sendagaya Japanese School, for the accredited preparatory course. The other two do not solve this.
  • Aiming at a master's? Sendagaya Japanese Institute — if your kanji is already at the level they require. [source:2]
  • Non-kanji background and aiming at graduate school? Start with the preparatory course and ask them about the route. [source:2]
  • Planning to work rather than study further? Sendagaya Language School. [source:3]
  • Just want to learn Japanese well? Any of them will teach you Japanese. But you would be paying for exam preparation or thesis writing you do not need, so say so when you enquire and let them point you at the right course.

Our profiles list what each one publishes: Sendagaya Japanese School, Sendagaya Japanese Institute and Sendagaya Language School. If you are weighing which intake month to target in the first place, see how the four intakes differ.

Course structures carry an effective-from date and change between academic years — the group's own pages are linked below and are the authority. Check them against the year you are applying for, and confirm capacity and intake months directly before you commit to anything.

claims_without_sources: 三校が別法人であるか、同一法人の別課程であるかという法的な関係 —— グループ站は三つのパスで別々の校名を出しているが、法人格の異同を明記していない。日振協の登録情報も突き合わせていないため、「one group」「three schools」とだけ書き、法人関係には触れていない。
定員 100 名の就職課程が「小規模ゆえにこうなる」という具体的な帰結 —— 他記事（ヒューマンアカデミー福岡）では規模の帰結を書いたが、ここでは三校の比較が主題なので、定員の対比を示すに留め、少人数の長短は論じていない。
各課程の学費 —— 2026-09 時点の人工確認どおり、グループ站に価格ページが存在しない。金額は一切書いていない。
「卒業時期がそろう」ことの学校側の意図 —— 課程長の一覧からは明らかだが、学校はその設計理由を説明していない。したがって事実（長さ）は出典付き、解釈（同じ時期に終わる＝走路の長さが変わるだけ）は出典なしとして書いた。
大学院進学コースが要求する「一定の漢字力」の具体的水準 —— 学校は水準を数値やJLPTレベルで示していない。したがって「they require」とだけ書き、N2 などの具体を補っていない。
